transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you—what has been bothering you lately that made you decide to come in today?

I’ve been having these obsessive, intrusive thoughts that won’t stop, and I feel like I have to do certain things over and over to calm myself down. It’s getting to the point where it’s really interfering with my day and I’m exhausted by it.

Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling mostly sad or unable to enjoy things you usually like, or is it more that you feel tense and worried all the time even when you’re not doing the rituals?

It’s more that I feel tense and on edge most of the time, even when I’m not actually doing the rituals. The obsessive thoughts—about things being contaminated, not safe, or “wrong” somehow—are always kind of in the background, and that makes it hard to relax or enjoy things, even though I wouldn’t say I’m constantly sad.

Aside from the obsessive thoughts and rituals, do you also find yourself worrying excessively about many different everyday things (like work, health, family, finances) most days, even when there’s no specific trigger, or is the anxiety mainly tied to the obsessions themselves?

I think the anxiety is mostly tied to the obsessions themselves—like when I start thinking something’s contaminated, unsafe, or that I’ve made some kind of mistake. I do worry about things like my health or whether I’ve done something wrong, but it usually feels connected to those specific thoughts rather than a constant, general worry about everything.

When these intrusive thoughts come up, do you recognize that they’re unreasonable or excessive, or do they feel realistic and you’re convinced the feared outcome will actually happen if you don’t do the rituals?

It kind of depends on the thought. With contamination or health stuff, in the moment it often feels very real, like “what if this actually makes me or someone else sick,” and I get pretty convinced something bad will happen if I don’t do the ritual. With some of the more taboo or “what if I hurt someone” thoughts, a part of me knows they’re irrational, but they still feel so disturbing that I act like they might be true just in case.
Over the last month, have there been most days when you felt clearly down or depressed for hours at a time, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, separate from the anxiety and obsessions?

I’m not really sure I’d call it clearly depressed most days. I do feel worn down and less interested in things because the anxiety and rituals take so much out of me, but I wouldn’t say I’m consistently low in mood for hours every day.

When you feel anxious or have these intrusive thoughts, do you feel driven to perform specific repetitive behaviors or mental rituals (like checking, washing, counting, or repeating phrases in your head) to reduce the anxiety, and do these take up a lot of time each day?

Yeah, I feel like I have to do certain things over and over to get the anxiety down. I wash my hands a lot, check locks and appliances repeatedly, line things up “just right,” and sometimes repeat certain phrases or prayers in my head, and altogether that can easily take one to two hours a day and makes me late or distracted with normal tasks.

When these thoughts and urges to do rituals come up, do you usually try to resist or delay doing the compulsions because you see them as unreasonable, or do they feel more like something you simply must do and you don’t really question them in the moment?

Most of the time they feel like something I just have to do in the moment, like an urgent pressure, and it’s really hard to think clearly about whether they’re reasonable. I do sometimes try to resist or delay, especially if I’m in public or running late, but the anxiety ramps up so much that I usually end up giving in just to get some relief.

On days when your obsessions and rituals are relatively mild or not happening much, do you still find yourself feeling generally anxious and worrying about lots of different everyday things most of the day, or does your anxiety mostly fade when the obsessions and rituals ease up?

When the obsessions and rituals ease up, my anxiety definitely goes down a lot. I might still have some normal worries about work or family, but I don’t feel that same constant, intense tension unless the obsessive thoughts are really active.
How long have you been experiencing these obsessive thoughts and rituals—are we talking weeks, months, or several years, and have there been periods when they went away or were much milder?

I’ve been dealing with them for several years now, probably since late high school or early college, but they’ve gotten noticeably worse over the past year or so. There have been stretches where they were milder or I could ignore them more, usually when life was less stressful, but they’ve never completely gone away.

Overall, do these obsessive thoughts and rituals feel unwanted and out of line with what you believe is reasonable (something you wish you could stop), or do you mostly feel they’re justified and necessary to stay safe?

They mostly feel unwanted and out of line with what I think is reasonable—I’m very aware they’re excessive and I wish I could just stop doing them. But in the moment they still feel necessary to keep myself or others safe, so it’s like my logical side and my anxious side are fighting with each other.

latest_inference.note: Previously the only candidate was F42, reflecting a working hypothesis of an obsessive–compulsive type condition. The current interview strongly supports this: the patient reports recurrent intrusive thoughts about contamination, harm, and things being "wrong"; recognizes them as excessive or unreasonable at least part of the time; and performs time‑consuming compulsions (washing, checking, ordering, mental rituals) aimed at reducing anxiety. Symptoms have been present for several years, cause clear distress and functional impairment, and are not better explained by a persistent low mood or a generalized, free‑floating worry pattern. The anxiety is closely tied to the obsessions and largely subsides when these are less active, which argues against adding a separate generalized anxiety condition. The patient does not describe a sustained depressive syndrome independent of the obsessions/compulsions, so a primary mood disorder is not added to the differential at this stage. Thus, no new major diagnostic candidates are introduced, and F42 remains the sole candidate.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts (contamination, harm, things being 'wrong') recognized as excessive and ego-dystonic, accompanied by repetitive compulsive behaviors and mental rituals (washing, checking, ordering, mental prayers) performed to reduce anxiety. These symptoms consume 1–2 hours daily, have persisted for several years, and cause clear functional impairment (lateness, distraction, exhaustion). Anxiety is largely contingent on the obsessions and markedly decreases when obsessions/rituals ease, arguing against a separate generalized anxiety disorder and supporting a primary diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42).
